title: Preparing a Wedding Brunch: Fruit Platters with a Mandoline
meta_description: Master fruit platter prep for wedding brunch with a mandoline slicer. Get pro-level, consistent fruit slices for a stunning, restaurant-quality display.
html:
When you're tasked with the catering for a wedding brunch, the pressure is on to make everything look effortless and elegant. One of the most visually impactful elements of a breakfast spread is the fruit platter. However, anyone who has spent an hour hacking away at a pineapple with a chef's knife knows that consistency is the hardest part. If some slices are thick and others are paper-thin, the platter looks homemade in a way that doesn't always fit the wedding aesthetic.

The secret to achieving that high-end, hotel-lobby look is all about precision. To streamline your fruit platter prep for wedding guests, you need a tool that removes the guesswork. That’s where a Mandoline Slicer comes in. By using a Mandoline Slicer, you can get restaurant-thin, even slices of fruit fast, ensuring every piece of melon or apple looks identical.

Choosing the Right Fruits for a Mandoline

Not every fruit is a candidate for the mandoline. You want items with a firm structure that can withstand the blade without turning into mush. For a wedding brunch, focus on fruits that hold their shape and offer a variety of colors to make the platter pop.

Firm melons—like cantaloupe, honeydew, and watermelon—are perfect. They provide a sturdy base and slice beautifully into uniform rounds or crescents. Apples and pears also work well, provided you toss them in a bit of lemon juice immediately after slicing to prevent browning. Avoid overly soft fruits like ripe peaches or berries on the mandoline; those are better left whole or quartered by hand.

Step-by-Step Fruit Platter Prep for Wedding Displays

To keep your kitchen organized and your fruit fresh, follow a systematic approach. The goal is to minimize the time the fruit spends exposed to air before it hits the platter.

  1. Prep the Station: Clear your counter and set out your platters. Have a bowl of citrus water (lemon or lime) ready for oxidizing fruits.
  2. Slice the Base: Start with your largest fruit, like watermelon. Use the Mandoline Slicer to create consistent rounds. These act as the structural foundation of your platter.
  3. Add Contrast: Switch to a different thickness setting on your adjustable mandoline for a different fruit, like honeydew, to create visual variety.
  4. The Detail Work: Slice firmer fruits like apples or hard pears into thin matchsticks or rounds for a delicate touch.
  5. Assembly: Instead of piling fruit in a heap, overlap the slices in a shingled pattern. This maximizes the surface area and makes the platter look abundant.

Safety First: Using the Hand Guard

If you've ever used a mandoline, you know the blades are incredibly sharp. When you're in the middle of a high-volume prep session for a wedding, it's easy to get complacent. This is why using the hand guard is non-negotiable.

The Mandoline Slicer comes with a dedicated hand guard that holds the fruit securely against the blade. As the piece of fruit gets smaller, the guard protects your fingertips from the edge. Never attempt to slice the last inch of a melon or apple without the guard; it’s simply not worth the risk. A few extra seconds of setup save you from a trip to the urgent care during wedding weekend.

Pro Tips for Platter Presentation

Once you have your perfectly even slices, the way you arrange them determines the final vibe. For a wedding, think about geometry. Instead of a random mix, try creating concentric circles of different colored fruits, starting with a mound of berries in the center and radiating outward with your mandoline-sliced melons.

To add a professional touch, garnish the gaps with fresh mint leaves or edible flowers. If you're serving the platter outdoors, keep the fruit chilled until the last possible moment. Because the slices from a Mandoline Slicer are so thin, they have more surface area and can dry out faster than thick chunks. A light spritz of lime juice not only adds flavor but keeps the fruit looking glistening and fresh.

Cleaning and Maintaining Your Slicer

Fruit sugars are sticky, and if they build up on the blade, your slices will start to tear rather than cut. Between different types of fruit, give your Mandoline Slicer a quick rinse under cold water. This prevents the flavors from mixing—you don't want your honeydew tasting like apple.

Once the wedding prep is finished, disassemble the slicer and wash it thoroughly. Since these tools have adjustable settings and moving parts, ensure they are completely dry before storing them to maintain the edge of the blade for your next event.

FAQ

Can I use a mandoline for soft fruits like kiwi?

Kiwi is borderline. If it's slightly under-ripe, a mandoline works great. If it's very soft, the blade will squash the fruit. For very soft fruits, stick to a sharp paring knife.

How do I stop sliced apples from turning brown on the platter?

Dip your slices in a mixture of cold water and lemon juice (about 2 tablespoons of juice per cup of water) for a few minutes before arranging them. This creates a barrier that slows down oxidation.

What is the best thickness setting for wedding fruit platters?

For melons, a medium thickness (around 1/8 to 1/4 inch) provides a good balance of aesthetics and stability. For apples or pears, go thinner (1/16 inch) to create a more elegant, translucent look.
